title: Partir, dormir, boire et sentir
summary: Distinguish short singular stems from fuller plural stems and use sentir for perception, smell and personal feelings.
objectives: Conjugate partir, sortir, dormir, sentir and boire.
Distinguish smelling something, giving off a smell and feeling well.

sections.title: A missing consonant returns in the plural
paragraphs: Partir (leave), sortir (go out), dormir (sleep) and sentir (smell/feel) do not follow finir. In the singular they lose the last stem consonant and use -s, -s, -t. The fuller stem returns with -ons, -ez, -ent. Derivatives such as repartir (leave again), ressortir (go out again) and endormir (put to sleep) keep these patterns in these meanings. Mentir (lie) follows the same type: je mens, tu mens, il/elle/on ment, nous mentons, vous mentez, ils/elles mentent.
points: Do not insert the regular -ir family's -iss-.

mistakes.why: Dormir does not belong to the finir family.
The singular stem drops t before the je ending -s.

sections.title: Boire has boi-, buv- and boiv-
paragraphs: Boire means drink. Its singular uses boi-, nous and vous use buv-, and ils/elles use boiv-. Un verre (m.) is a glass; du lait means some milk. A drink taken in an unspecified quantity normally has a partitive article.
points: Je bois and il boit sound alike but have different final letters.

sections.title: The construction tells you who senses what
paragraphs: Sentir can mean perceive by smell or touch: je sens la fumée means I can smell the smoke; je sens le froid means I feel the cold. A thing can be the subject when it gives off a smell: la soupe sent bon means the soup smells good. Here bon and mauvais act as unchanging adverbs, not adjectives agreeing with the noun.

Se sentir describes how a person feels: je me sens bien, elle se sent fatiguée. The little word me or se points back to the subject; the next lesson on reflexives teaches the full system. For now contrast sensing something with describing one's own state.
points: La fumée (f.) = smoke; une fleur (f.) = a flower; le froid (m.) = cold.

examples.note: Like partir, sentir restores its full stem in the plural.
The flowers give off the smell; bon does not become bonnes.
Se sentir reports the subject's own state.
Sentir + a noun can identify the smell given off.

mistakes.why: In sentir bon, bon is an invariable adverb.

practice.prompt: Choose the sentence meaning 'I feel well'.
practice.explanation: The reflexive form describes your state.
Repartir restores the full stem in the plural.
The singular form is dort, without m.
Vous uses the full sent- stem.

practice.prompt: Supply bon or bonnes: 'Ces roses sentent ___.'
practice.explanation: Bon is invariable in sentir bon.

practice.prompt: In 'La cuisine sent le pain', is the kitchen smelling something with a nose or giving off a smell?
practice.explanation: A place as subject can be described as smelling of something.
Mentir restores t in the plural.

practice.prompt: Supply the missing pronoun for 'I feel tired': 'Je ___ sens fatigué.'
practice.explanation: Se sentir describes the subject's own state.
The plural restores the sort- stem.

production_task.prompt: Write a morning message saying how you feel, what you are drinking and when your group leaves.
production_task.model_answer: Je me sens bien. Je bois un café. Nous partons à neuf heures.
production_task.translation: I feel well. I am drinking a coffee. We leave at nine o'clock.
rubric: Use me with se sentir for a personal state.
Use partons, not a finir-style ending.
